# Probability Distributions You Will Actually Use

| Distribution | Models | Where it appears in CS |
|--------------|--------|-------------------------|
| Normal | Symmetric noise | Aggregated metrics, central-limit results |
| Log-normal | Multiplicative effects | Latency, file sizes, response times |
| Exponential | Memoryless waiting times | Inter-arrival times in queueing |
| Poisson | Count of rare events | Bug arrivals, packet counts |
| Binomial | Successes in *n* trials | Pass/fail of test cases |
| Pareto | Heavy tails | Web request sizes, network flows |
| Student's *t* | Sampling distribution of the mean | Small-sample inference |
| χ² | Sum of squared normals | Goodness-of-fit, contingency tables |
| *F* | Ratio of variances | ANOVA |

```r
rnorm(10, mean = 0, sd = 1)
dnorm(0)               # density at 0
pnorm(1.96)            # P(Z <= 1.96)
qnorm(0.975)           # 97.5th percentile
```

## The Central Limit Theorem in One Picture

```r
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(1)
sim <- replicate(10000, mean(rexp(30, rate = 1)))
ggplot(data.frame(m = sim), aes(m)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "tomato", colour = "white") +
  labs(title = "Sample means of n=30 from Exp(1)",
       x = "sample mean")
```

Even though we sampled from a strongly skewed exponential, the distribution
of the *mean* is approximately normal. This is why so many classical tests
are robust when *n* is reasonably large.
